title: Seneca's rehearsal
hook: rehearse losses ahead of time so they don't ambush you (Letters 91)

segments.voice: Yesterday: memento mori, remember you will die, so the middle is spent well. Your line was one of a limited number.

News reached Rome that the city of Lugdunum, today's Lyon in France, had burned to the ground. A prosperous, handsome city, gone in a single night. Seneca had a friend from Lugdunum named Liberalis, and Liberalis was devastated, not only by the loss but by the shock of it. He had never seen it coming. Seneca wrote about it in a letter to another friend, Lucilius, describing a practice that can soften a blow like that. It sounds strange at first: think about disasters on purpose, before they happen.
screen: `A CITY BURNS IN ONE NIGHT.` → `LIBERALIS, DEVASTATED.` → `THINK OF IT BEFORE IT HAPPENS.`

segments.voice: Premeditatio means thinking ahead. Modern writers often add malorum: premeditatio malorum, thinking ahead about hard things. Cicero discusses the idea too, in his Tusculan Disputations. In Letter 91, Seneca says, in paraphrase, that nothing should be unexpected by us. Send the mind out ahead to meet everything that could happen, not only what usually happens but what can. Exile, illness, war, shipwreck. The blow that's been foreseen, he says, lands lighter. What hurts most is the ambush: the loss that arrives when we'd assumed it never could. This can sound like a recipe for anxiety, so here's what it is not. It isn't worrying. Worry replays the same fear over and over, with no end and no plan. Seneca's rehearsal is short and deliberate. You picture a loss, calmly, once. You notice that you could survive it, and what you'd do. Then you come back to today and notice the loss hasn't happened. Your job is still here. Your friend is still alive. The city is still standing. Modern Stoic writers such as William Irvine call this negative visualization, and they stress that return: the rehearsal makes what you have look less guaranteed, and so more precious. Seneca's version came out of a real fire, in a real city, and a friend in grief.
screen: `NOTHING SHOULD BE UNEXPECTED.` · `SEND THE MIND OUT AHEAD.` · `NOT WORRY: ONCE, CALMLY, THEN BACK.` · `WHAT YOU HAVE LOOKS PRECIOUS.` · then, large: `FORESEEN IS LIGHTER.`

segments.voice: Keep it small today: picture losing something minor, your phone, a favorite mug, a day's plans canceled, and see it happen, calmly. Notice that you would manage, and you'd know what to do. Then come back, the phone still here, the mug still on the shelf, and let the picture go, glad of the ordinary thing that's still yours.
Premeditatio. Latin for thinking ahead: rehearsing losses briefly, so they don't ambush you. Today's word.
Your line: foreseen is lighter. It's the ambush that hurts most. That's day one hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism use a brief rehearsal of possible losses, following Seneca's Letter 91, picturing a setback calmly and then returning to what they still have.

original.note: Latin: thinking ahead, rehearsing in the mind. The full phrase praemeditatio malorum means thinking ahead about hard things.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: SERIOUS fix: Letter 91 is addressed to Lucilius, not to Liberalis; the hook, fork and source said Seneca wrote to Liberalis. Also cut 'around the year 64' and 'two thousand years old' (not in the cited letter); the 'return' to gratitude is now credited to modern writers (Irvine), not presented as Seneca's; the garbled claim that the practice itself 'came out of' the fire was fixed (Cicero discusses it earlier); 'the part people forget' cut.
The index word is 'premeditatio' (without the Latin ae); the original game uses the classical spelling 'praemeditatio'. Confirm.
Letter 91 is paraphrased; confirm that Liberalis was from Lugdunum, the fire's date (c. 64–65 CE), and the list of misfortunes (exile, illness, war, shipwreck) in Seneca's text.
Cicero Tusculan Disputations 3 section numbers for praemeditatio futurorum malorum, and his tracing it to the Cyrenaics/earlier Greeks: confirm.
The distinction between rehearsal and worry, and the note that some therapists use a version of it, are this script's framing; a clinician may want to check that it is not presented as therapy.
